content: A powerful magnitude 6.6 earthquake struck the Banda Sea off eastern Indonesia early on Tuesday, shaking remote island communities around the city of Tual and sending tremors as far as Darwin in northern Australia, according to the United States Geological Survey (USGS). No casualties or serious damage had been reported by Tuesday morning, and no tsunami warning was issued. The earthquake struck at 21:11 UTC on Monday, which was 06:11 local time on Tuesday in Tual, with its epicentre about 148 kilometres west-southwest of the city at a depth of 68 kilometres beneath the sea, [the USGS said](https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/eventpage/us7000tymu). It was the strongest earthquake recorded anywhere in the world in the past 24 hours. The tremor arrived on a week when global attention is already fixed on Asia ahead of the first trilateral summit between the leaders of China, the United States and Russia, [due to open in Shenzhen on November 19](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/xi-trump-putin-summit-shenzhen-november-19). One of the first things many readers will have noticed is that the earthquake did not have a single agreed magnitude. The USGS put it at 6.6, Indonesia's own Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysical Agency (BMKG) recorded it at 7.1, and Geoscience Australia initially reported 7.4. The differences are normal in the first hours after a large earthquake, and they say more about how earthquakes are measured than about the ground itself. Each agency works from a different set of seismic stations, and early automated readings are revised as more data arrives. Depth matters too: the USGS placed the quake 68 kilometres down, BMKG put it at 115 kilometres, and the Australian reading placed it at just 29 kilometres. A deeper earthquake spreads its energy over a wider area but usually shakes the surface less violently at any one point, which helps explain why a quake of this size caused so little damage. BMKG said the earthquake had no tsunami potential, a conclusion supported by its depth and by the fact that the sea floor moved mostly sideways rather than lifting a large column of water. The agency reported weak shaking at intensity III in Tual, Saumlaki, Tiakur, Dobo, Sorong, Manokwari, South Manokwari, Bintuni, Fakfak and Kaimana, and at intensity II in Nabire and Serui. Those are levels at which people indoors feel the movement and hanging objects swing, but buildings are not expected to suffer damage. Across the sea in Australia, the tremor was felt hundreds of kilometres from the epicentre. Hundreds of Australians reported feeling the shaking after it reached the northern city of Darwin at around 6:41 a.m. local time, and the Bureau of Meteorology confirmed there was no tsunami threat to mainland Australia or its islands. The USGS issued a Green alert for the event, its lowest level, meaning there is a low likelihood of casualties or economic losses. Its models estimated that about 8,100 people were exposed to moderate shaking, with a similar number feeling lighter shaking, and no population exposed to the most violent shaking. Ten felt reports had been filed with the USGS within hours of the quake. Tual is a port city on Kei Kecil island in Maluku province, in the far east of the Indonesian archipelago, and the waters around it are among the most seismically active on Earth. Indonesia sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where the Australian, Pacific and Eurasian tectonic plates meet, and the Banda Sea in particular is a complex junction of colliding plates that produces frequent large earthquakes. Most of them strike far offshore and deep underground, as this one did, which is why many pass with little more than a scare. That geography is also why the numbers deserve a second look. A magnitude 6.6 earthquake directly beneath a city would be a very different event from the same magnitude 148 kilometres offshore and 68 kilometres down, and the early reports from Tual and the surrounding islands suggest this one fell firmly into the second category. Local authorities were still checking for damage in the hours after the quake, and residents were advised to stay alert for aftershocks, which commonly follow an earthquake of this size over the following days. Neither the USGS nor BMKG had reported any casualties by Tuesday morning, and no tsunami warning was in force. The figures may still be revised as more seismic data is analysed, and both agencies said they would update their assessments if damage reports emerge from the remote islands nearest the epicentre.
summary: A magnitude 6.6 earthquake struck the Banda Sea off eastern Indonesia early on Tuesday, shaking communities around Tual in Maluku province and sending tremors as far as Darwin in northern Australia; no casualties or serious damage were reported and no tsunami warning was issued.
title: Magnitude 6.6 earthquake strikes off Indonesia's Tual, shaking islands and reaching Australia
